**The operator compresses nothing it puts on a socket.** Not `/api/*` JSON, not
the sync read path, not SPA assets, not docs HTML. If you are adding a response
path, send the bytes raw. `npm run lint:no-wire-compression` fails the build if
you don't.

This is the conclusion of WI-5988 (owner directive, 2026-07-26). It is worth
knowing *why*, because "add gzip, it's free bandwidth" is a reflex that will
otherwise keep coming back.

## Why

Papercusp ships as a **Tauri desktop app**. The operator host binds `127.0.0.1`
(`resolveBindHost`) and every consumer — the desktop webview, the Vite dev
browser, local agents — is on the same machine. Compression trades CPU for
bandwidth, and over loopback **there is no bandwidth to buy**: you are spending
real milliseconds on both ends to shrink bytes that never leave the box.

Two parts of the codebase had already reached this conclusion independently,
years apart, without anyone generalising it:

- `src-tauri/src/custom_protocol.rs` strips `accept-encoding` from every
  relayed request outright — *"Loopback has ..."*.
- `pty-ws.ts` sets `perMessageDeflate: false` — *"we send mostly small frames,
  deflate adds latency"*.

And the one genuinely **remote** consumer, the mobile client on `/device/*`,
never compressed at all.

## What it measured

Measured on the real `plans.list` payload through the real `:3170` path — not a
synthetic buffer:

| | |
|---|---|
| payload | 764.1 KB raw → 156.6 KB gzip (**4.88x**) |
| gzip, server CPU | **12.54 ms** per response |
| gunzip, client CPU | **2.94 ms** per response |
| loopback transfer of the extra bytes | **1.41 ms** (loopback measured at 3.5 Gbit/s) |
| **net** | **14.07 ms worse per response — an 11x bad trade** |

Note the shape of that result: the loopback saving is **not zero**. A
back-of-envelope that treats loopback as free predicts ~150x; the real number is
11x. Still decisive, but if you are re-litigating this, *measure* — the reason
this entry exists is that the original gzip was added on an estimate
(*"agentRunsSheets.all is 85 KB raw vs 12 KB gzipped, and Zero polls it every
3s"*) that was never re-checked. Zero has since been retired; the justification
outlived the thing it was justifying.

### The tell that should have caught it earlier

`cpu-task-worker.ts` — an entire `worker_threads` subsystem — was built in part
because `gzipSync` blocked the main event loop 50–100 ms per call. We stood up a
thread pool to *hide the cost of work that did not need doing*. When you find
yourself building infrastructure to make something cheap enough to tolerate, ask
whether it needs to happen at all.

(The worker survives, and still earns its keep: `JSON.stringify` on a 3.5 MB
payload is 30–50 ms of real, unavoidable work. Only the gzip half was removed.)

## What is still compressed, deliberately

The guard is narrow on purpose. **Decompression is always fine** — reading a
gzipped log or a zstd archive blob is normal. And all of this **at-rest /
distribution** compression is correct and stays:

- `packages/backup` — gzipped `pg_dump` output
- `session-archive.ts` — zstd session-archive blobs
- `llm-testing/storage.ts` — zstd transcripts in PG
- `deployment/runtime-pack.ts`, the installer payloads — tarballs
- `dev-source-extract.ts` — zstd source bundle
- `infra/defguard/Caddyfile` — `encode gzip` on a **real network hop**

That last one is the rule for the future: **if a real network hop ever appears
in front of the operator, compress at the edge proxy.** `content-encoding` is a
transport concern and belongs where the transport actually costs something —
not baked into an app whose clients are all `127.0.0.1`.

## The guard

`scripts/check-no-wire-compression.mjs` (`npm run lint:no-wire-compression`,
gating in CI) scans the transport layer — `apps/operator/bin`,
`endpoint-route`, `libs/generic/sync/src`, plus the sync/pty transport files —
for compression **producers**: `hono/compress`, a zlib compressor,
`CompressionStream`, a compressed `content-encoding` response header,
`perMessageDeflate: true`. Decompressors never match, and comments explaining
the ban don't trip it (there is a `--self-test` for the matcher).

The unit tests are **inverse guards**: `http-routes.test.ts` and
`cpu-task-worker.test.ts` assert that a response carries **no**
`content-encoding` *even when the client sends `accept-encoding: gzip`*. So
re-adding compression reds a test with a clear message rather than being
discovered in a CPU profile six months later.
